label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files) and its 55-page PDF built at 893dadaf
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 01 Slides as a compromise: two pages on why slides are a compromise and Bret Victor before any factory appears; I am a team member with an agent already, I wanted the team first.
02 The tour: seven stops of screenshots of a site I will never use; I skimmed to the 'What the tour leaves out' end.
08 The plumbing: the register's 320 claims and the corrections file that said 'None yet' are for a book team, not for my stand team; I took only the 'one check' line.
09 The loop and the port: the storyteller, the objection and the port are a long afternoon of one man's talk; I skimmed.
10 to 11: the last ten minutes and what did not work are honest and good, but the minute-by-minute detail of the lock and the parts is for people who were there; I took the lesson lines and moved on.
13 Sessions end: useful idea (a role is not a session) but I read it on one pass.
15 Principles: a recap of what I had just read; I skipped to chapter 16.
first_thing_i_would_do: Write one page of rules and one brief for my own agent, plus the hold's two lines (who pulls, who lifts when the owner is away), and send them round the stand team before any of us start work.
price: about 8 pounds as a short practical book; I would pay nothing for 55 pages in this order and would want the last third first
why: The method is good and copyable: a page of rules, a brief, a check, a hold anyone can pull, a status file and debrief for every agent. But I had to read 40 pages of one day's story to reach the part I could use, and the chapter where it becomes about several people at once (14) is a plan, not something that ran. The book itself says the third factory 'has not run yet'. My question was whether our team could run like this, each of us with our own agent, and the book answers it honestly with 'not tested'. I like the honesty, but I need the team pattern earlier and with more on it.

by_chapter.why: Strong voice note and the 'pressing play' point, but it is about slides and the author's frustration, not my team. The takeaway (write your one idea) arrives only at the end.
by_chapter.quote: I was the bit in between.

by_chapter.why: Seven screenshots of a site tour. Good proof that it ran, no method in it. Several 'Figure to come' boxes make it thin on the page.
by_chapter.quote: Every rule on my page cost somebody a slide.

by_chapter.why: First practical chapter: the page of rules shown, the reality file, the check and the brake. This is where I started taking notes. The shop-owner example is exactly the right size.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: Roles with a scope and a mistake behind each rule; the scope is a setting and not a boundary is the sentence I will repeat to my team. The empty security chair is a good hook.
by_chapter.quote: A scope is a setting, not a boundary

by_chapter.why: The five-step wake with a real wake walked through, including the partial verdict. Reviewer is a second reading, not a second identity. Directly copyable.
by_chapter.quote: Partial is a true answer. Done would have been a nicer one.

by_chapter.why: Requests as files, notes in commits: the nearest thing to what my team could adopt tomorrow. I wanted it earlier and longer.
by_chapter.quote: a request is a file, and the answer is a file

by_chapter.why: The hourly chart helps; the picture round-trip between deck and ruv-sgit is charming but long. The ephemeral-container point is the useful bit.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: Four pipes is a good frame, but the claims register and corrections file are book-team specifics. The one check that would have saved you last time is the takeaway.
by_chapter.quote: Gaps are allowed. Hiding them is not.

by_chapter.why: Port, not rebuild is a real lesson but buried in a long afternoon. The relayed-word refusal is the best moment and is told again in chapter 15.
The hold at 18:44 is vivid and the file is shown. Fair to the conductor. 'I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.' is the line that sold me on the brake.
by_chapter.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.

by_chapter.why: The failures at full size are what make me trust the rest: lock never turned, correction lost in the freeze. The 'write down what waits to go in when you unfreeze' lesson is practical.
by_chapter.quote: when you freeze something, write down what is waiting to go in when you unfreeze it.

by_chapter.why: Honest answer to what contained it, with a state-machine picture. Thin in places, but the line that controls fail by not being switched on is true of my own team.
by_chapter.quote: Most controls do not fail because someone defeats them. They fail because nobody gets round to switching them on.

by_chapter.why: Role versus session is a useful idea, but the worked handover is about the book's own storyteller and its accounts. I wanted a template I could copy.
by_chapter.quote: A member of the team is a role

by_chapter.why: The chapter my persona cares about most, and the weakest: a plan for the Web Summit team that has not run. One brief owner, a board read each morning, a hold anyone pulls. The corrected-line scene and the evening lost to the usage limit are good. The deal-breaker is nearly met: one brief with one owner and a conductor in the middle.
by_chapter.quote: Two people editing one brief is how a team ends up with two briefs.

by_chapter.why: Six principles with their sources are tidy and quotable but repeat chapters 3 to 11. I would fold them into chapter 16.
by_chapter.quote: I do not trust principles that arrive without a story.

by_chapter.why: The chapter I would photograph. Five steps, a shop owner's example, a checklist of every do-this-now. Step 5 (a second agent only when the first is busy; two agents allowed the same file will collide) is the team advice, in one line.
Short and useful as a glossary I can hand to a colleague who has not read the rest. Fine at the back.

p54: the checklist's fourteen long lines in small type
best_line: Nobody needs permission to stop. Everybody needs his to start again.
worst_moment: Chapter 2, the tour: seven stops of screenshots of a talk site and a book team's own pages, with several empty Figure boxes, before I have been told how I would run my own team; no takeaway until the one-line 'Do this now'.
versus_the_thirty: If I had only the thirty pages I would already have the method and the five steps. The seventy adds the failures at full size, which I do trust more, a worked wake, the mail and board, and the hold's two lines for several people. It also adds the long middle (tour, plumbing, loop, port) that I do not need. For my team the extra I want is more on chapter 14 and nothing else; the rest I would take as optional reading.
top_three_changes: Put the team pattern up front: move 'one brief, one board, one hold' and the three-roles-to-start advice into chapter 3 or earlier, and draw the three-people picture (p49) so a team reader finds themselves in the first twenty pages.

Make chapter 14 run, or say clearly what has not been tested: add the Web Summit team's first week, even as a dated list of what the first day will look like, plus one named person who lifts the hold, so the method does not depend on one editor and one conductor.

Cut or merge for a reader like me: fold chapter 15 into 16, trim 2, 8 and 9 to a page each, and draw the 'Figure to come' boxes that carry the method (p53 five steps, p54 checklist, p21 wake record, p49 shared things).
notes: Fictional persona on a phone between meetings, five minutes of attention: the PDF is the wrong shape for me and I read the pages as a scroll. The honesty about failures, 'Do this now' at the end of every chapter and the shop-owner example won me; the single editor who signs for everything is the thing I would need to change for a team of people. No em-dashes, no religious words in this note.
